hooks.text: Astronomers mailed physical hard drives to photograph our galaxy's terrifying center.
Why did scientists mail hard drives to see a black hole?
To photograph our galaxy's giant black hole, scientists couldn't use the internet.

title: The Terrifying Truth of Our Galaxy's Black Hole
description: The supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy is a sleeping giant. When astronomers finally photographed Sagittarius A*, they couldn't even use the internet to send the data.

beats.text: Astronomers mailed physical hard drives to photograph our galaxy's terrifying center.
beats.visual: Illustration of global networks connecting to a central point

beats.text: Discovered in 1974, Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole at our galactic center.
beats.visual: Panoramic view of the Milky Way galaxy highlighting the galactic center, 2020

beats.text: It has a mass about four million times our Sun, hidden behind thick cosmic dust.
beats.visual: Infrared view of cosmic dust in the central Milky Way, 2015

beats.text: About 350 years ago, this quiet beast released a million times more energy than today.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a highly active supermassive black hole with flares, 2018

beats.text: In 2017, the global Event Horizon Telescope captured the glowing ring around its shadow.
beats.visual: ALMA antennas pointing at the night sky in Atacama Desert, 2017

beats.text: But gas orbits this small target so fast that its appearance changed in mere minutes.
beats.visual: Simulation of hot gas orbiting rapidly around a supermassive black hole, 2021

beats.text: The resulting flood of scientific data was too massive to send over the internet.
beats.visual: Stacks of high capacity hard drives at Max Planck Institute, 2018
subjects: Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy

beats.text: Instead, five years of complex processing finally revealed the direct image in May 2022.
beats.visual: First direct radio image of the Sagittarius A* black hole, 2022

beats.text: No network on Earth could easily transmit the secrets of our galaxy's lurking beast.
beats.visual: Wide field view of the Sagittarius constellation and Milky Way center, 2021

better_than_last: This episode tests using a surprising logistical challenge as the hook to spark immediate curiosity about an astronomical mystery, aiming to lift retention in the first ten percent.
